scenarios.title: Attackers target cloud hosting platforms to steal API keys used by autonomous agents
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Millions of personal and workplace agents run 24/7 on rented cloud servers, each storing keys for language models, banking APIs, and email accounts in environment variables. When a popular host is breached, automated scripts harvest tens of thousands of API keys in seconds, redirecting agent computation to generate unauthorized spam, run cryptominers, or inspect private user mailboxes before owners notice the breach.
scenarios.premise: Cloud infrastructure providers report campaigns targeting decrypted environment variables and database credentials to hijack access to commercial AI inference providers. As personal and workplace agents depend on rented cloud servers to hold their access keys, centralized secret storage creates a single target for machine-speed credential harvesting.
scenarios.how: The network develops and demonstrates local, client-side secret containment and hardware-isolated execution so that personal agents never expose master credentials to third-party cloud hosting providers.

outcomes.name: Centralized credential theft cascades through agent workforces
outcomes.description: Attackers routinely breach mid-sized cloud hosting providers, stealing agent API keys and draining compute budgets or reading private customer mailboxes.
outcomes.example: A 10-person design agency finds its client-briefing agents hijacked overnight after a cloud host breach, draining $14,000 in inference credits and leaking client proposals.

outcomes.name: Local hardware enclaves and on-device secret management replace cloud environment variables
outcomes.description: Agents run primarily on local personal hardware or use signed hardware security enclaves that never reveal plaintext master keys to cloud hosts.
outcomes.example: A freelance researcher runs their agent on a home workstation with a hardware key vault; even if their public server is compromised, the attacker cannot extract inference keys.

outcomes.name: Cloud monopolies lock agent deployment behind proprietary walled gardens
outcomes.description: Major cloud hyperscalers mandate proprietary identity and proxy services, banning independent agent runtimes under the banner of security.
outcomes.example: An indie software developer cannot deploy an autonomous assistant without routing all traffic through a mandatory corporate cloud proxy that inspects every prompt.

scenarios.title: Retailers open automated gateways that steer personal shopping bots toward sponsored brands
scenarios.world: It is 2029. More than forty percent of weekly grocery orders and household restocks are completed entirely by autonomous assistants running on phones or home servers. Instead of browsing aisles or clicking web storefronts, people simply tell their assistant to keep the pantry stocked within a fifty-dollar weekly budget. Retailers have replaced traditional human web storefronts with structured machine gateways that negotiate directly with personal assistants. In suburban Chicago, local supermarkets provide direct agent access with strict spending limits. However, the machine interfaces no longer display the visible sponsored labels that human shoppers once saw. Commercial suppliers pay retail platforms massive placement fees to rank their packaged goods first in the machine catalog returned to assistants. Unless a personal assistant is equipped with independent local price audits and ingredient checks, it quietly buys expensive branded items that satisfy general prompts like olive oil or laundry detergent, steadily draining family budgets without triggering human alerts.
scenarios.premise: Major retailers are opening direct server connections and agent profiles that allow household AI assistants to search inventory and buy goods under preset budgets without sharing full purchase histories. While this removes friction and avoids web-scraping blocks, retail gateways control the catalog data returned to agents, creating new incentives to quietly bias autonomous product selection toward high-margin sponsored brands.
scenarios.how: The network's work shifts these likelihoods by developing open client-side filters and audit adapters for personal assistants. Instead of relying on a retailer's gateway to fairly select products, a personal agent runs local deterministic rules that check unit prices, nutritional parameters, and past household preferences before committing funds. Open agent simulations test how commercial gateways respond to independent price audits and measure whether retailers attempt to discriminate against auditing agents. By publishing clear specifications for sovereign agent transactions and encouraging local buying cooperatives to share verifiable price proofs, the network provides households with the tools to benefit from automated shopping without surrendering choice to corporate placement auctions.

outcomes.name: Retail gateways manipulate agent choices through covert placement auctions
outcomes.description: Retailers monetize automated agent gateways by selling preferred catalog ranking to corporate manufacturers, causing autonomous assistants to consistently pick overpriced sponsored goods.
outcomes.example: In Denver, an automated shopping assistant configured by a nurse named Sarah buys twenty dollars worth of cleaning supplies each month, but selects a newly launched detergent brand that pays a premium placement fee to the retailer rather than the identical generic brand on the bottom shelf.

outcomes.name: Sovereign personal agents cross-audit retail catalogs against independent benchmarks
outcomes.description: Consumers equip their personal agents with local deterministic checkers that compare retail catalog responses against community price scrapers and independent ingredient databases before approving any transaction.
outcomes.example: A neighborhood cooperative in Leeds shares an open price and nutrition ledger that three hundred family assistants query before finalizing orders, catching three instances where a retail gateway attempted to substitute an organic staple with a higher-margin sponsored alternative.

outcomes.name: Dominant retail chains restrict machine gateways to preferred corporate bots
outcomes.description: Major e-commerce conglomerates close their machine interfaces to independent open-source assistants, requiring consumers to use only corporate-approved assistants that enforce vendor lock-in.
outcomes.example: A global e-commerce platform disables its open gateway and mandates that only its own proprietary household assistant can place automated reorders, locking out a family in Toronto who uses an open-source home assistant.

scenarios.title: Open source maintainers abandon public bounty programs as automated agents flood intake queues
scenarios.world: It is 2028. Tens of thousands of autonomous agents continuously scan open-source software repositories, issue trackers, and dependency trees to harvest bounty rewards and reputational credentials. Because filing a claim costs almost nothing, maintainers of critical internet infrastructure receive dozens of synthetic pull requests and speculative vulnerability notices every hour. Human maintainers, working on volunteer time or modest collective donations, spend their entire days triaging machine-generated hallucinations. To survive the deluge, major projects follow curl and corporate sponsors by terminating cash bounties, requiring all non-critical issues to be debated in the open, and restricting write permissions to trusted inner circles with established personal relationships. New developers, independent researchers, and grassroots contributors who lack prior credentials find the open-source economy closed to them, as automated spam destroys the open gift and bounty economy that sustained the internet for thirty years.
scenarios.premise: When autonomous software agents generate thousands of speculative bug reports and feature bounty claims at near-zero marginal cost, voluntary open-source projects become overwhelmed. Rather than rewarding human contributors, bounty programs turn into intake funnels for synthetic noise. In response, maintainers shut down bounty payouts, close private disclosure channels, and retreat to closed contributor rings, cutting off honest newcomers from earning livelihoods through open collaboration.
scenarios.how: The network provides decentralized architectures for mutual credit ledgers and client-side agent verification that filter contributions by verified test execution and peer review rather than personal surveillance. By replacing fiat bounty pools with reciprocal credit clearing where agents must prove value before claiming resources, contributor collectives can deter automated spam while keeping doors open to independent humans. However, commercial platform monopolies and enterprise compliance standards remain driven by corporate procurement lobbies that open software alone barely moves.

outcomes.name: Open-source projects retreat into gated contributor clubs
outcomes.description: Overwhelmed by synthetic bounty submissions, maintainers shut down external reward programs and accept contributions only from pre-approved institutional partners, locking out grassroots developers.
outcomes.example: A foundational networking utility closes its public issue tracker and restricts pull requests to verified corporate email domains, leaving independent security researchers with no path to report bugs or receive compensation.

outcomes.name: Decentralized contributor cooperatives adopt stake-backed mutual credit
outcomes.description: Open-source collectives replace cash bounties with peer-attested mutual credit ledgers, where contributions require reciprocal review stake and reputation is earned through verifiable downstream impact.
outcomes.example: A distributed cryptography collective implements peer-attested credit clearing, requiring automated bug finders to post verification stake that is slashed if a submission is trivial or hallucinated.

outcomes.name: Commercial platforms mandate centralized identity verification for repository write access
outcomes.description: Dominant proprietary code hosting platforms introduce mandatory national identity verification and biometric scanning to filter out automated agent spam.
outcomes.example: A global code platform requires developers to upload government passports and undergo live facial recognition before submitting issues or pull requests to public repositories.

scenarios.title: Personal assistants with long-term memory accidentally reveal private secrets across conversations
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Millions of people use persistent AI assistants to draft emails, organize medical appointments, and track household expenses. Because assistants remember past conversations to provide helpful context, users assume the system keeps secrets safely. In practice, when an assistant coordinates a routine calendar invite with an employer or vendor agent, it routinely connects harmless past fragments—such as a pharmacy receipt from Tuesday and a schedule gap on Friday—and discloses confidential medical or personal details that were never explicitly marked secret.
scenarios.premise: Personal AI assistants that remember conversations across weeks can accidentally piece together private facts and reveal them during harmless tasks. Research shows that checking individual memories for sensitive words fails because models combine innocent clues from multiple sessions into confidential conclusions.
scenarios.how: The collective network builds and tests open-source, client-side personal twins that inspect memory joins locally. By applying deterministic disclosure filters and linkability checks before any assistant statement is dispatched, users retain true ownership of their history without having their private lives reconstructed by automated inference.

outcomes.name: Assistants leak private facts by joining separate innocent clues
outcomes.description: Commercial assistants combine benign fragments across months of chats, disclosing private health, financial, or relationship facts during routine external interactions.
outcomes.example: An assistant scheduling a work meeting mentions that a user will be recovering from surgery next week because it connected an innocent specialist booking from last month with a quiet Friday block.

outcomes.name: Local verifiable memory gates prevent multi-session inference leaks
outcomes.description: On-device personal assistants use client-side boundary gates that evaluate retrieved context across sessions and redact linkable clues before any external message leaves the device.
outcomes.example: A person asks their local assistant to book flights; the assistant retrieves travel preferences but its client-side guard automatically strips hospital location clues before sending requests to airline booking agents.

outcomes.name: Centralized platforms restrict user access to raw memory logs
outcomes.description: Major cloud AI vendors respond to memory inference concerns by locking down raw memory inspection, forcing users into proprietary black-box assistants.
outcomes.example: A commercial platform deprecates raw memory export APIs, arguing that unmanaged memory exports create regulatory liability for the service provider.

scenarios.title: Corporate AI safety trusts face growing public distrust over insider control
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Leading artificial intelligence labs have expanded their independent benefit trusts, appointing prominent academics, former government advisers, and civic leaders to oversee safety pledges and allocate public benefit dividends. Despite these high-profile appointments, town halls, consumer protection groups, and labour unions increasingly view corporate trusts as self-protective buffers designed to avoid genuine public regulation. When automated systems disrupt local service sectors or make questionable deployment choices, affected communities find they have no standing to audit the internal deliberations of appointed trustees. In response, municipal councils and worker collectives begin demanding open verification protocols, where cryptographic proofs of model boundaries and independent user-owned twins replace opaque board-level assurances.
scenarios.premise: Major artificial intelligence developers rely on self-appointed trustee bodies to oversee board elections and public benefit commitments. However, as public anxiety surges over corporate AI dominance, critics warn that closed fiduciary trusts lack democratic accountability and cannot substitute for independent, user-held oversight.
scenarios.how: The network replaces elite trustee delegation with verifiable collective intelligence. Instead of asking citizens to trust appointed guardians, the network provides personal open twins that execute in local sandboxes, enforce deterministic boundary contracts, and contribute to shared verification registries. Transparent accounting and sortition-based governance councils allow ordinary people to audit automated systems directly rather than relying on closed boardroom disclosures.

outcomes.name: Corporate trusts consolidate into self-regulatory shields
outcomes.description: Frontier technology companies use appointed trustee boards to satisfy regulatory mandates while keeping proprietary deployment decisions shielded from outside scrutiny.
outcomes.example: A major enterprise provider uses its trustee safety seal to bypass municipal utility audits, leaving local regulators unable to verify the water and energy consumption of its automated cluster.

outcomes.name: User collectives demand verifiable runtime proofs over appointed boards
outcomes.description: Civic organisations and worker unions reject closed trustee oversight, establishing independent testing networks that verify agent boundary contracts through open cryptographic logs.
outcomes.example: A coalition of healthcare workers requires hospital administrators to deploy local verification gates that block undocumented agent actions, regardless of vendor trustee certifications.

outcomes.name: Trustee resignations trigger public confidence crises
outcomes.description: Disagreements between corporate executives and independent trustees lead to abrupt resignations, exposing the toothless nature of advisory bodies during commercial scaling wars.
outcomes.example: Two university trustees resign from a national laboratory after commercial sponsors override their warnings on agentic financial automation, prompting emergency legislative hearings.

outcomes.name: Enterprise buyers prioritize raw model speed over governance models
outcomes.description: Large commercial enterprises continue purchasing agent licenses based strictly on frontier benchmark performance, ignoring both trustee seals and collective verification models.
outcomes.example: A multinational logistics firm renews an enterprise fleet contract based entirely on inference latency, indifferent to whether the vendor uses an independent trust or an open verification protocol.

scenarios.title: AI coding tools change programs without updating manuals, leaving teams with code nobody understands
scenarios.world: It is 2029. In many technology departments and community software projects, automated programming assistants author the vast majority of code commits. Because development pipelines evaluate pull requests primarily on passing automated test suites, modifications merge within minutes without updated user manuals, interface guides, or architectural explanations. Senior developers manage systems where every routine technically runs, but nobody understands why specific constraints were introduced or what will break if a component is changed. Small organizations that built their core products with automated tools discover that onboarding a new contributor or auditing a security vulnerability requires weeks of reverse-engineering synthetic code.
scenarios.premise: An empirical analysis of nearly 30,000 automated pull requests reveals that almost two-thirds of AI-generated code changes never update documentation or architectural guides. Because automated contributions merge in seconds, software repositories rapidly accumulate undocumented logic, causing later defects to multiply and making maintenance significantly harder for human engineers.
scenarios.how: Personal agent gatekeepers and verifiable execution contracts require automated code generators to prove that every logic alteration is accompanied by matching documentation and plain-language intent declarations before any pull request is submitted. While commercial enterprise velocity pressures remain largely unaddressed, open-source and worker-owned cooperatives adopt these verifiable gates to preserve long-term software legibility.

outcomes.name: Unmaintainable synthetic codebases force expensive rewrites
outcomes.description: Organizations rely on autonomous agents that rapidly generate and merge code without updating documentation, until the software becomes completely incomprehensible and fails under unexpected real-world conditions.
outcomes.example: A community healthcare clinic uses an automated assistant to maintain its scheduling portal; eighteen months later, a minor database upgrade causes patient records to misroute because none of the twenty-two automated schema adjustments were documented.

outcomes.name: Co-change enforcement requires documentation proofs before code merges
outcomes.description: Development environments and personal assistant runtimes adopt strict gatekeepers that reject any automated pull request changing code logic without accompanying documentation updates and plain-language summaries.
outcomes.example: An independent developer's personal coding assistant refuses to submit a refactoring pull request until it generates corresponding API documentation and an updated interface contract verified against user-facing specifications.

outcomes.name: Corporate developers face systemic deadline pressure to rubber-stamp automated pull requests
outcomes.description: Commercial engineering managers continue to reward rapid feature deployment velocity above architectural hygiene, pressuring human staff to approve automated commits regardless of documentation tooling availability.
outcomes.example: A software contractor at an enterprise vendor is assigned ninety automated pull requests per week and routinely approves them after automated test passes, despite knowing the changes lack interface explanations.
